claim: The Drosophila lymph gland is the major hematopoietic organ that develops during the larval stages for the purpose of providing blood cells during later pupal/adult periods.
source: The Drosophila lymph gland is the major hematopoietic organ that develops during the larval stages for the purpose of providing blood cells during later pupal/adult periods (reviewed in Banerjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Banerjee et al., 2019).

claim: Hematopoietic function for the larva itself is largely provided by a separate set of sessile or circulating blood cells outside of the lymph gland.
source: Hematopoietic function for the larva itself is largely provided by a separate set of sessile or circulating blood cells outside of the lymph gland (reviewed in Letourneau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Letourneau et al., 2016).

claim: The only time the lymph gland provides blood cells to the circulating larval hemolymph is if the larva faces a stress or immune challenge.
source: The only time the lymph gland provides blood cells to the circulating larval hemolymph is if the larva faces a stress or immune challenge.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The PSC (Posterior Signaling Center) is marked by expression of Antp.
source: The PSC (Posterior Signaling Center) is marked by expression of Antp (Mandal et al., 2007) and knot/collier (kn/col) (Crozatier et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Mandal et al., 2007).

claim: The PSC is marked by expression of knot/collier (kn/col).
source: The PSC (Posterior Signaling Center) is marked by expression of Antp (Mandal et al., 2007) and knot/collier (kn/col) (Crozatier et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research (Crozatier et al., 2004).

claim: Progenitors belong to the medullary zone (MZ) and are marked by domeMESO and Tep4.
source: The PSC signals progenitors that belong to the medullary zone (MZ) and are marked by domeMESO and Tep4 (Jung et al., 2005; Irving et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Jung et al., 2005; Irving et al., 2005).

claim: Differentiating cells form the cortical zone (CZ), expressing Hemolectin (Hml), Peroxidasin (Pxn), lozenge (lz), and other differentiating cell markers.
source: Differentiating cells form the cortical zone (CZ), expressing Hemolectin (Hml), Peroxidasin (Pxn), lozenge (lz), and other differentiating cell markers (Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research (Jung et al., 2005).

claim: A narrow band of cells that are double positive for domeMESO and HmlΔ occupy the edge abutting the MZ and CZ in the early third instar.
source: A narrow band of cells that are double positive for domeMESO and HmlΔ occupy the edge abutting these two zones in the early third instar (Sinenko et al., 2009), and is referred to as the intermediate zone (IZ), which contains intermediate progenitors (IPs) (Krzemien et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Sinenko et al., 2009).

claim: The intermediate zone (IZ) contains intermediate progenitors (IPs).
source: A narrow band of cells that are double positive for domeMESO and HmlΔ occupy the edge abutting these two zones in the early third instar (Sinenko et al., 2009), and is referred to as the intermediate zone (IZ), which contains intermediate progenitors (IPs) (Krzemien et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research (Krzemien et al., 2010).

claim: Drosophila blood cells are all similar in function to cells of the vertebrate myeloid lineage.
source: Invertebrates predate the evolution of the lymphoid system for adaptive immunity. Accordingly, Drosophila blood cells are all similar in function to cells of the vertebrate myeloid lineage.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about invertebrate immunity and evolutionary relationships.

claim: Plasmatocytes (PLs) represent 95% of all hemocytes.
source: The most predominant class of blood cells, the plasmatocytes (PLs; 95% of all hemocytes), share a monophyletic relationship with vertebrate macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Plasmatocytes share a monophyletic relationship with vertebrate macrophages.
source: The most predominant class of blood cells, the plasmatocytes (PLs; 95% of all hemocytes), share a monophyletic relationship with vertebrate macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about evolutionary relationships.

claim: PLs function in the engulfment of microbes and apoptotic cells.
source: PLs function in the engulfment of microbes and apoptotic cells, and they produce extracellular matrix proteins (Fessler and Fessler, 1989; Tepass et al., 1994; Franc et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Fessler and Fessler, 1989; Tepass et al., 1994; Franc et al., 1996).

claim: PLs produce extracellular matrix proteins.
source: PLs function in the engulfment of microbes and apoptotic cells, and they produce extracellular matrix proteins (Fessler and Fessler, 1989; Tepass et al., 1994; Franc et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Fessler and Fessler, 1989; Tepass et al., 1994; Franc et al., 1996).

claim: Crystal cells (CCs) represent 2–5% of hemocytes.
source: A minor (2–5%), but important class is represented by crystal cells (CCs) named for their crystalline inclusions of the pro-phenoloxidase enzymes, PPO1 and PPO2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: CCs are named for their crystalline inclusions of the pro-phenoloxidase enzymes, PPO1 and PPO2.
source: A minor (2–5%), but important class is represented by crystal cells (CCs) named for their crystalline inclusions of the pro-phenoloxidase enzymes, PPO1 and PPO2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: CCs are necessary for melanization.
source: CCs are necessary for melanization, blood clot formation, immunity against bacterial infections, and to help mitigate hypoxic stress (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).

claim: CCs are necessary for blood clot formation.
source: CCs are necessary for melanization, blood clot formation, immunity against bacterial infections, and to help mitigate hypoxic stress (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).

claim: CCs are necessary for immunity against bacterial infections.
source: CCs are necessary for melanization, blood clot formation, immunity against bacterial infections, and to help mitigate hypoxic stress (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).

claim: CCs help mitigate hypoxic stress.
source: CCs are necessary for melanization, blood clot formation, immunity against bacterial infections, and to help mitigate hypoxic stress (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rämet et al., 2002; Galko and Krasnow, 2004; Binggeli et al., 2014; Dudzic et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018).

claim: The transcription factor Lozenge (Lz) cooperates with Notch signaling to express a number of target genes (such as hindsight/pebbled) to specify CCs.
source: The transcription factor Lozenge (Lz) cooperates with Notch signaling to express a number of target genes (such as hindsight/pebbled) to specify CCs (Lebestky et al., 2000; Duvic et al., 2002), whereas the Sima (vertebrate HIF-1α) protein is required for their maintenance (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Lebestky et al., 2000; Duvic et al., 2002).

claim: The Sima (vertebrate HIF-1α) protein is required for CC maintenance.
source: The transcription factor Lozenge (Lz) cooperates with Notch signaling to express a number of target genes (such as hindsight/pebbled) to specify CCs (Lebestky et al., 2000; Duvic et al., 2002), whereas the Sima (vertebrate HIF-1α) protein is required for their maintenance (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research (Mukherjee et al., 2011).

claim: The orthologue of Lz in mammals is RUNX1.
source: The orthologue of Lz in mammals is RUNX1, with broad hematopoietic function at many developmental stages, and RUNX1 is often dysregulated in acute myeloid leukemias (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).

claim: RUNX1 has broad hematopoietic function at many developmental stages.
source: The orthologue of Lz in mammals is RUNX1, with broad hematopoietic function at many developmental stages, and RUNX1 is often dysregulated in acute myeloid leukemias (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).

claim: RUNX1 is often dysregulated in acute myeloid leukemias.
source: The orthologue of Lz in mammals is RUNX1, with broad hematopoietic function at many developmental stages, and RUNX1 is often dysregulated in acute myeloid leukemias (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (de Bruijn and Speck, 2004; Ito, 2004).

claim: Lamellocytes represent <1% of blood cells and are usually present only during parasitization by wasps.
source: The third class of blood cells, lamellocytes (<1%), is usually present only during parasitization by wasps (reviewed in Letourneau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Letourneau et al., 2016).

claim: A small number of cells clustered near the heart (dorsal vessel) are identified as pre-progenitors.
source: In early genetic studies, the MZ appeared to consist of a fairly homogeneous group of cells, although a small number of cells clustered near the heart (dorsal vessel) are identified as pre-progenitors (Jung et al., 2005; Dey et al., 2016; Tiwari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Jung et al., 2005; Dey et al., 2016; Tiwari et al., 2020).

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity and complexity within the progenitor population.
source: More recent reports have noted considerable heterogeneity and complexity within the progenitor population (reviewed in Banerjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Banerjee et al., 2019).

claim: There is a functional distinction into a Hh-sensitive and a Hh-resistant group of progenitors within the MZ.
source: Particularly noteworthy, in this context, is the functional distinction into a Hh-sensitive and a Hh-resistant group of progenitors within the MZ (Baldeosingh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research (Baldeosingh et al., 2018).

claim: Progenitors are maintained through PSC-derived signals and through a signaling relay mediated by the differentiating cells.
source: In brief, progenitors are maintained not only through PSC-derived signals but also through a signaling relay mediated by the differentiating cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The backward signal from the differentiating cells to the precursors is named the Equilibrium Signal.
source: This backward signal from the differentiating cells to the precursors is named the Equilibrium Signal (Mondal et al., 2011; Mondal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Mondal et al., 2011; Mondal et al., 2014).

claim: Pvf1 produced by the PSC trans-cytoses through the MZ to bind its receptor Pvr, which is expressed at high levels in the CZ.
source: In this process, Pvf1 (PDGF- and VEGF-related factor 1) produced by the PSC, trans-cytoses through the MZ to bind its receptor Pvr (PDGF/VEGF receptor), which is expressed at high levels in the CZ.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pvr binding initiates a STAT-dependent but JAK-independent signaling cascade that ultimately leads to the secretion of the extracellular enzyme ADGF-A.
source: This initiates a STAT-dependent but JAK-independent signaling cascade that ultimately leads to the secretion of the extracellular enzyme ADGF-A (adenosine deaminase-related growth factor A).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: ADGF-A breaks down adenosine, preventing its mitogenic signal and proliferation of MZ progenitors.
source: This enzyme breaks down adenosine, preventing its mitogenic signal and proliferation of MZ progenitors.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The niche and the backward signal maintain a balance between progenitor and differentiated cell types.
source: Acting together the niche and the backward signal maintain a balance between progenitor and differentiated cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Bulk RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted cells identifies new blood cell subpopulations along a developmental trajectory with multiple paths to mature cell types.
source: Using a combination of bulk RNA-Seq of FACS-sorted cells, single-cell RNA-Seq, and genetic dissection, we identify new blood cell subpopulations along a developmental trajectory with multiple paths to mature cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including bulk RNA-Seq and scRNA-Seq results.

claim: Metabolism is a driver of development in the lymph gland.
source: We highlight metabolism as a driver of development, show that graded Pointed expression allows distinct roles in successive developmental steps, and that mature crystal cells specifically express an alternate isoform of Hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif/Sima).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including metabolic gene expression analysis.

claim: Graded Pointed expression allows distinct roles in successive developmental steps.
source: We highlight metabolism as a driver of development, show that graded Pointed expression allows distinct roles in successive developmental steps, and that mature crystal cells specifically express an alternate isoform of Hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif/Sima).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including genetic analysis of pnt function.

claim: Mature crystal cells specifically express an alternate isoform of Hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif/Sima).
source: We highlight metabolism as a driver of development, show that graded Pointed expression allows distinct roles in successive developmental steps, and that mature crystal cells specifically express an alternate isoform of Hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif/Sima).

claim: The Musashi-regulated protein Numb facilitates Sima-dependent non-canonical Notch signaling.
source: Mechanistically, the Musashi-regulated protein Numb facilitates Sima-dependent non-canonical, and inhibits canonical, Notch signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including genetic analysis of numb and msi function.

claim: Numb inhibits canonical Notch signaling.
source: Mechanistically, the Musashi-regulated protein Numb facilitates Sima-dependent non-canonical, and inhibits canonical, Notch signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript and established knowledge about Numb function.

claim: Prior to making a fate choice, a progenitor selects between alternative, biologically relevant, transitory states allowing smooth transitions reflective of combinatorial expressions rather than stepwise binary decisions.
source: Broadly, we find that prior to making a fate choice, a progenitor selects between alternative, biologically relevant, transitory states allowing smooth transitions reflective of combinatorial expressions rather than stepwise binary decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including trajectory and pseudotime analysis.

claim: The view that progenitors select between alternative transitory states is gaining support in mammalian hematopoiesis.
source: Increasingly, this view is gaining support in mammalian hematopoiesis.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of recent trends in mammalian hematopoiesis research.

claim: MZ progenitors are validated by their expression of domeMESO-EGFP, col (collier), Tep4, shg (shotgun; E-Cad), and dome (domeless).
source: MZ progenitors are validated by their expression of: domeMESO-EGFP, col (collier), Tep4, shg (shotgun; E-Cad), and dome (domeless); CZ plasmatocytes (PLs) by: HmlΔ-DsRed, Hml (Hemolectin), Pxn (Peroxidasin), vkg (viking), Col4a1, and NimC1; and the crystal cells (CC; also part of CZ) by: lz (lozenge), hnt (hindsight/pebbled), PPO2, and PPO1.
